doc: The five rules a rider's hand-curated list is assembled from, and survives on. A favourite is a route AT a boarding pole (ADR-032) keyed on the *member* pole id rather than the churning `P:` place id (ADR-062), so the screen's job is to turn a rider's hand-curated list of keys into cards: `migrateFavouriteKeys` brings a list written by an older scheme up to date — the one rule in this repo whose failure loses something a rider made by hand, which is why it is versioned rather than merely changed; `favouritePoleIds` says which poles to fetch, a question the screen must answer BEFORE it has any data; and `favouritesView` says what the cards contain, grouped by the place each saved pole resolves to. TWO MORE ARE ABOUT THE BLOB RATHER THAN THE SCREEN: `mergeSavedKeys` and `mergePreferences` reconcile two writers of the one `nextbus.preferences` blob — a second tab, the other app on the same origin, a tab restored from the back/forward cache — against the ancestor they diverged from, which is what lets a removal be told from an addition without a tombstone. Their payloads are plain blobs rather than dataset extracts, because a preferences blob IS the whole of what they see. Every payload below is a **trimmed** real one from the live dataset — real canonical ids, real names in all three locales, real service facts — with only the route rows a case needs and every reading re-timed against a fixed `now` of 2026-08-05T00:30:00+08:00, because a fixture that read a clock would be worthless to a second platform. TWO ROWS RECORD BUGS THIS GROUP CLOSED (WP6-4b) rather than bugs it carries — a saved route with no live reading is a row now, and a line saved at two kerbs is two rows — and each says in its `why` what it used to do. No row here is `knownDefect`.

migrateFavouriteKeys.doc: v0 → v1: a favourite saved against a merged `P:` place id becomes one key per member pole, in save order. Every member, never a guess at one — a place-keyed favourite does not say which kerb the rider meant, and the screen intersects the saved keys with the rows a place actually reports, so an over-expanded key can never render while a wrong guess is an invisibly missing favourite.

cases.name: a-place-keyed-favourite-becomes-one-key-per-member
cases.why: The migration proper. The place id names three members, so one saved key becomes three — and the route id is carried through unchanged.

cases.name: a-pole-keyed-favourite-passes-through
cases.why: The overwhelmingly common case even in a v0 blob: most favourites were saved from a lone stop or from a route schematic, which have always keyed on the pole.

cases.name: an-expansion-that-lands-on-a-saved-key-does-not-duplicate-it
cases.why: A rider who saved the route at the place AND at one of its kerbs. Two identical keys would render as two rows of one line, which is the bug the de-duplication exists for.

cases.name: a-key-the-grammar-cannot-read-is-kept-verbatim
cases.why: Not deleted, and not quarantined. Today's grammar is narrower than tomorrow's — a fifth operator ships and the id pattern widens — the render path already skips what it cannot parse, and a key that starts parsing again later simply starts working again.

cases.name: a-blob-already-at-the-current-version-is-untouched
cases.why: The step must not run twice. It is idempotent anyway, but skipping it is what makes "run once and stamp the blob" true rather than "fix up on every read", which never finishes and leaves no evidence the scheme ever moved.

cases.name: a-blob-from-a-future-version-is-untouched
cases.why: A rider who downgraded, or two tabs on different builds. A scheme we cannot read renders as nothing, which is recoverable by upgrading again; discarding it is not.

cases.name: a-version-that-is-not-a-number-is-treated-as-the-oldest
cases.why: A hand-edited or truncated blob. One comparison, and the alternative failure is a list that silently skips every step it needed.

mergeSavedKeys.doc: Two writers' favourite lists, reconciled against the ancestor they diverged from. `base` is the writer's OWN previous list, which is what makes a deletion and an addition tell apart: a key missing from `mine` was un-starred here, one missing from `theirs` was un-starred there, and either deletion beats the other side's stale copy. Everything else is a union, ordered `theirs` first then this writer's own additions so that two writers that have seen each other converge on identical bytes. ONE PRECONDITION, which is the caller's and cannot be a type: `theirs` must have been read AFTER `base` was written. An ancestor that has run ahead of the snapshot makes this writer's own addition look exactly like the other writer's deletion — the last row below is that shape, and it is a real defect (WP6-8b), not a hypothetical one.

cases.name: an-addition-on-each-side-is-kept
cases.why: The ordinary two-tab case: a rider stars one route here and another there before either write is seen. Both survive, and the order is theirs-then-mine — which is what stops the two tabs writing the same set back to each other in their own orders forever.

cases.name: a-removal-here-survives-the-other-tabs-stale-copy
cases.why: The row a set-union cannot pass, and the reason `base` exists at all. Un-star a route in this tab and the other tab still has it in memory; under a union it would come straight back, so a rider with two tabs open could never delete a favourite.

cases.name: a-removal-in-the-other-tab-is-applied-here
cases.why: The same rule from the other side, and the half a naive "keep everything I have" would fail. The other writer deleted it; this writer never touched it; it goes.

cases.name: the-same-key-starred-on-both-sides-appears-once
cases.why: Two tabs showing the same place, both stars tapped. A duplicate key is not merely untidy: the Favourites screen treats the list as a set, so an un-star that removed one copy would appear to do nothing.

cases.name: a-key-both-writers-dropped-stays-dropped
cases.why: Idempotence for a deletion. The second tab has already applied the removal, so neither side holds the key any more and the merge must not reason it back into existence from the ancestor.

cases.name: with-no-shared-ancestor-nothing-is-removed
cases.why: A writer that has never persisted passes an empty ancestor, which says "I have deleted nothing" — so the merge is a pure union. Anything else would let a freshly-loaded tab delete a list it has never seen.

cases.name: an-ancestor-ahead-of-theirs-reads-an-addition-as-a-deletion
cases.why: The precondition, violated — and the row that says where the fix belongs. `base` names a key this writer has just added while `theirs` is a snapshot taken before that write landed, so `base \ theirs` reads as "the other writer deleted it" and the rider's own star is erased. Both stores did exactly this before WP6-8b: two taps in one task, an unseen key on disk, and a favourite gone from memory and disk with no second tab involved. The arithmetic here is CORRECT and must not be softened — dropping the `base \ theirs` half would leave a rider with two tabs open unable to delete a favourite at all, which is the bug `base` exists to avoid. What has to hold instead is the caller's sequencing: read, merge, write and adopt in one critical section, and advance the ancestor only with the write.

mergePreferences.doc: The whole blob, merged: `base` is this writer's previous persisted state, `mine` is what it holds now with its change included, `theirs` is what is on disk right now. Scalars go to whichever side moved away from the ancestor, with the local side winning a true conflict; favourites are merged key by key; the recents follow the scalar rule as WHOLE lists, because an MRU order cannot be interleaved. A `null` here is a value and not the corpus's usual absent marker: `theirs: null` means nothing is on disk, `base: null` means this writer has never persisted, and `localeOverride: null` means follow the device.

cases.name: a-writer-that-changed-nothing-adopts-the-other-tabs-blob
cases.why: The reproduction, from the receiving side: the other tab changed the language and starred a route, this one has done nothing since it loaded, so every field falls to the other tab's. This is the whole of what a `storage` listener is for.

cases.name: a-choice-made-here-beats-the-other-tabs-older-one
cases.why: The write side of the same rule, and the half that must not be "adopt whatever arrived": the rider's finger was on this tab a millisecond ago. Both scalars and both recents lists moved here, so all four keep the local value; the other writer adopts them when its own event lands.

cases.name: a-star-here-and-a-language-there-both-survive
cases.why: `docs/07`'s reproduction in one call — the exact interleaving that used to revert a language change when the second tab starred a route. The favourite is this writer's addition and the language is the other's, and the merge is not allowed to choose between them.

cases.name: an-unstar-here-is-not-resurrected-by-the-other-tab
cases.why: The deletion carried through the whole blob rather than through the key list alone, because this is the call the stores actually make. Nothing else moved, so the result differs from `mine` only in the field the other tab is stale about.

cases.name: a-reordered-recents-list-is-a-local-change
cases.why: An MRU bump is a reorder, not a growth, so sameness has to be order-sensitive: a length-only comparison would treat "the rider just opened this route again" as no change and hand the list back to the other tab.

cases.name: a-writer-that-loaded-before-the-blob-existed-adopts-it
cases.why: `base` is null: this writer has never persisted, so its values are defaults rather than choices and it cannot have deleted anything. Adopting the disk wholesale is right here and wrong everywhere else, which is why the absence is a separate input rather than an empty blob.

cases.name: no-blob-on-disk-leaves-this-writer-untouched
cases.why: `theirs` is null — a first run, or another app calling `localStorage.clear()`. There is nobody to merge with, so the rider's own state stands. Emptying it here would be the same data loss from the opposite direction.

cases.name: two-writers-that-already-agree-have-nothing-to-merge
cases.why: The steady state, and the row that pins the identity return: every field is equal, so the merge yields `mine` itself. The stores read that identity as "there is nothing to write and nobody to notify", which is what stops two tabs handing an unchanged blob back and forth forever.

favouritePoleIds.doc: Which poles the screen fetches, in save order, de-duplicated — one query returns a whole place, so two saved poles of one place must not fetch it twice. A key the grammar cannot read is skipped rather than resolved to a pole the rider did not save.

cases.name: two-poles-of-one-place-are-two-queries-in-save-order
cases.why: The ordinary shape. They are two distinct poles, so both are asked about; the place they resolve to is the wire's answer, not this rule's, so it cannot collapse them here.

cases.name: two-routes-at-one-pole-are-one-query
cases.why: One `getStop` returns every route at every kerb, so asking twice would double the request count for a rider who saved two lines at their local stop — the commonest list there is.

cases.name: an-unreadable-key-is-skipped-not-guessed-at
cases.why: It stays on disk (see the migration group) and contributes no query. Resolving it would mean fetching a pole the rider never saved.

cases.name: nothing-saved-is-nothing-to-ask
cases.why: The empty state, and it is the same answer as a list of keys none of which can be read — which is right: to a rider, both are a screen with nothing on it.

favouritesView.doc: One card per saved PLACE, in save order, carrying only the rows the rider saved — intersected at the pole, so opposite-kerb directions of one route number stay distinct (ADR-042). No `routeCount` and no `distanceM`: Favourites knows what the rider saved, not what serves the place, and distance is irrelevant on a screen opened from anywhere. The rows are sorted soonest-first and NOT capped here: the cap is the served `maxRows`, applied by `stopCardView` together with the "+N more" count.

cases.name: two-saved-poles-of-one-place-are-one-card
cases.why: The grouping decision, and the reason it is a place rather than a pole: a rider who saved two lines at two kerbs of one interchange saved two things at ONE place, and two cards would read as two places. Rows sorted soonest-first across both kerbs.

cases.name: a-saved-route-with-no-reading-is-still-a-row
cases.why: **The bug this row was written to record, now fixed (WP6-4b).** It read `knownDefect` until 2026-08-05: a route the rider saved with no live reading right now — a peak-only service at 23:00, which is most of a list overnight — contributed *nothing*, so the card was a name with nothing under it, and the consequence that mattered was diagnostic: it could not be told from a favourite key that no longer resolves. That is why WP5-11's favourites proof had to rest on a route with a live arrival. A saved route is a row now, whether or not a bus is due, and its readout is the timetable's published frequency, else a dash — the same three-way choice `PlaceRouteRow` has carried since WP6-3a. Found by WP5-11, declared as a `mustNot` in `StopRow`'s spec at WP6-1, closed here.

cases.name: one-line-saved-at-two-kerbs-is-two-rows
cases.why: WP5-12's residual, from the favourites side (ADR-072), and **the label was declined on a measurement**. A rider who stars one line at *both* kerbs of a place made an explicit choice, and the compact card used to collapse them into one row — right for a card summarising a place, wrong for a list the rider curated, and it hid the other kerb's bus entirely. Two rows now, each carrying its own reading. Naming the kerbs was tried: across five Hong Kong neighbourhoods **not one** line published at two kerbs of a place had *distinct* printed codes on them, and it could not, because a place's poles are clustered by sharing a name and the code is part of the name — both poles in this very row print `TN510`, which is ADR-071's own example. A label repeated on both rows claims a distinction it does not make, so there is none; Place detail, which has room for ADR-080's ladder, is one tap away.
